questions.question: Which of the following algorithms is NOT an example of uninformed search?
questions.explanation: Uninformed (blind) search algorithms explore the search space using no problem-specific knowledge beyond the raw structure of the graph/tree — they don't use any heuristic estimate of how close a state is to the goal. BFS, DFS, and Depth-limited Search are all classic examples of uninformed search, exploring purely based on the search tree's structure. A* Search , however, explicitly uses a heuristic function [latex]h(n)[/latex] (an estimate of the remaining cost to the goal) combined with the path cost so far, [latex]f(n)=g(n)+h(n)[/latex], to guide its search — making it an informed search algorithm, not uninformed. questions.question: Which of the following statements is NOT true? (The names of the predicates are intuitive.)

options.A: [latex]\forall x \forall y[/latex] Classmate [latex](x, y) \Rightarrow[/latex] Classmate [latex](y, x)[/latex]
options.C: "Each king is a person" is equivalent to [latex]\forall x \operatorname{IsKing}(x) \wedge \operatorname{IsPerson}(x)[/latex]
options.D: "All humans are mortal" is equivalent to [latex]\forall x \operatorname{IsHuman}(x) \Rightarrow \operatorname{IsMortal}(x)[/latex]

questions.explanation: Checking each statement: - "Classmate is symmetric" ([latex]\forall x\forall y\,\text{Classmate}(x,y)\Rightarrow\text{Classmate}(y,x)[/latex]): reasonably true given the intuitive meaning of "classmate." - "Everyone likes ice cream" phrased via a double negative ([latex]\forall x\,\text{Likes}(x,\text{Icecream})\Rightarrow\neg\exists x\,\neg\text{Likes}(x,\text{Icecream})[/latex]): this is a valid logical equivalence (universal statement restated using negated existential), true. - "Each king is a person" as [latex]\forall x\,\text{IsKing}(x)\wedge\text{IsPerson}(x)[/latex] : this is WRONG — using [latex]\wedge[/latex] (AND) here incorrectly asserts that everything in the domain is both a king and a person. The correct translation of "each king is a person" requires an implication : [latex]\forall x\,\text{IsKing}(x)\Rightarrow\text{IsPerson}(x)[/latex]. Using AND instead of implication is a classic FOL translation error. - "All humans are mortal" via implication ([latex]\forall x\,\text{IsHuman}(x)\Rightarrow\text{IsMortal}(x)[/latex]): this is the textbook-correct form, true. Answer: "Each king is a person" is equivalent to ∀x IsKing(x)∧IsPerson(x) (this statement is NOT true). Click Here for Detail Solution

questions.question: Consider that the quick sort algorithm is used to sort an array of [latex]n[/latex] distinct randomly ordered elements. In every call, the pivot is chosen as the first element of the current subarray. Let [latex]T(n)[/latex] denote the expected time to sort the array. Assume that the time to partition is linear in the size of the current subarray. Which of the following recurrence relations correctly represents [latex]T(n)[/latex] in this scenario?
questions.explanation: With the pivot always chosen as the first element , and the input array being randomly ordered (so the pivot's rank is uniformly random among the [latex]n[/latex] elements of the current subarray), the pivot ends up at position [latex]k[/latex] (splitting into a left part of size [latex]k[/latex] and right part of size [latex]n-k-1[/latex]) with equal probability [latex]1/n[/latex] for every [latex]k=0,1,\ldots,n-1[/latex]. Averaging over all these equally likely splits gives the expected-case recurrence : [latex]T(n)=\dfrac1n\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\big[T(k)+T(n-k-1)\big]+O(n)[/latex] The other recurrences describe specific worst-case ([latex]T(n)=T(1)+T(n-1)+O(n)[/latex], when the pivot always lands at an extreme end) or idealized-balanced ([latex]T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n)[/latex]) scenarios, not the true randomized average case. Answer: [latex]T(n)=\frac1n\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}[T(k)+T(n-k-1)]+O(n)[/latex] Click Here for Detail Solution

With the pivot always chosen as the first element, and the input array being randomly ordered (so the pivot's rank is uniformly random among the [latex]n[/latex] elements of the current subarray), the pivot ends up at position [latex]k[/latex] (splitting into a left part of size [latex]k[/latex] and right part of size [latex]n-k-1[/latex]) with equal probability [latex]1/n[/latex] for every [latex]k=0,1,\ldots,n-1[/latex].

Averaging over all these equally likely splits gives the expected-case recurrence:
[latex]T(n)=\dfrac1n\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\big[T(k)+T(n-k-1)\big]+O(n)[/latex]

The other recurrences describe specific worst-case ([latex]T(n)=T(1)+T(n-1)+O(n)[/latex], when the pivot always lands at an extreme end) or idealized-balanced ([latex]T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n)[/latex]) scenarios, not the true randomized average case.

Answer: [latex]T(n)=\frac1n\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}[T(k)+T(n-k-1)]+O(n)[/latex]

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true for Ridge Regression?

options.A: The regularizer in the objective function of Ridge Regression is used to guard against scenarios where the model works well for the test data, but poorly for the training data.
options.B: The regularizer of Ridge Regression uses [latex]L_{1}[/latex] norm.
options.C: Ridge Regression aims to reduce the number of parameters that have negative values.
options.D: The regularizer of Ridge Regression may increase the bias of the model, but it helps in reducing the variance in predictions.

questions.explanation: Ridge Regression adds an [latex]L_2[/latex] penalty (squared magnitude of weights), not [latex]L_1[/latex], to the loss function — ruling out the [latex]L_1[/latex]-norm option. It doesn't specifically target negative-valued parameters either. The core, textbook effect of this [latex]L_2[/latex] penalty is the classic bias-variance tradeoff : shrinking the weights towards zero makes the model slightly less able to perfectly fit the training data (increasing bias), but makes it much less sensitive to fluctuations in the training data (reducing variance) — usually a net win for generalization, especially when the unregularized model would otherwise overfit. Answer: The regularizer of Ridge Regression may increase the bias of the model, but it helps in reducing the variance in predictions. Click Here for Detail Solution

questions.question: Consider a directed graph [latex]G=(V, E)[/latex], where [latex]V[/latex] is the finite set of vertices and [latex]E[/latex] is the set of directed edges between the vertices. [latex]G[/latex] may contain cycles but there is no self-loop. Further, [latex]G[/latex] may not be strongly connected. Let [latex]G^{R}[/latex] be the graph obtained by reversing the directions of all the edges in [latex]G[/latex] without changing the set of vertices. Assume that Breadth First Search (BFS) or Depth First Search (DFS) from any given vertex [latex]v[/latex] of a graph visits only the reachable vertices from [latex]v[/latex] in that graph. Which of the following statements must always be true, regardless of the structure of [latex]{G}?[/latex]

options.A: If [latex]u[/latex] is a reachable vertex in the BFS of [latex]G^{R}[/latex] from [latex]v[/latex], then [latex]u[/latex] is also a reachable vertex in the DFS of [latex]G[/latex] from [latex]v[/latex].
options.B: In [latex]G^{R}[/latex], the BFS traversal from [latex]v[/latex] will visit exactly the same set of vertices as the DFS from [latex]v[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex].
options.C: The order of vertices visited in the BFS of [latex]G^{R}[/latex] from [latex]v[/latex] is the reverse of the order of vertices visited in the DFS of [latex]G[/latex] from [latex]v[/latex].
options.D: If [latex]u[/latex] is a reachable vertex in the DFS of [latex]G[/latex] from [latex]v[/latex], then [latex]v[/latex] is also a reachable vertex in the BFS of [latex]G^{R}[/latex] from [latex]u[/latex].

Reversing every edge along this path gives a directed path [latex]u\to v[/latex] in [latex]G^R[/latex] (by the very definition of the reversed graph). So [latex]v[/latex] is guaranteed reachable from [latex]u[/latex] in [latex]G^R[/latex] — regardless of whether BFS or DFS is used to actually discover this (both correctly find all reachable vertices, just possibly in different orders).
